_metadata.independence: I read only u23-blind-input.json; no other file, search, web lookup or API was consulted.

hints.reason: Honey is sweet (taste), but nothing about a star is sweet; the star side has no route.
Honey is golden in colour and 'gold star' is a familiar phrase; a shared-property colour route like SWEET for APPLE+HONEY.

best_available.why: The only hint that reaches both words; golden honey and gold stars are both everyday images.

pairs.pair_note: Thin pair; GOLDEN carries it alone and SWEET is honey-only filler.

hints.reason: Trains carry cargo, but honey is not recognisably cargo to a player; train-only.
Honey bun is a familiar compound/endearment, but there is no route from bun to train.

best_available.why: Neither hint reaches both words; CARGO at least admits honey as freight a train could carry, which BUN cannot do for train at all.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. Each hint is a one-sided compound; the pair needs a genuinely shared scene (e.g. a dining-car or a shared name) that neither hint supplies.

hints.reason: Honey dissolves in water: a verb route where honey is the thing dissolving and water the solvent.
Honey and lemon is a classic remedy pairing; lemon water is a familiar drink.
Honey is stirred into tea; tea is made with boiling water.

best_available.why: The most everyday scene: honey, lemon and hot water all meet in a cup of tea.

pairs.pair_note: Strong pair; all three hints live in the same kitchen scene.

hints.reason: The witch's gingerbread house in Hansel and Gretel is a famous scene; gingerbread is traditionally sweetened with honey (honey gingerbread/Lebkuchen), a moderate link.
Contains the target HONEY as a substring (rule failure) and has no route to witch anyway.
Witches brew potions, but honey as a potion ingredient is not a recognisable scene; witch-only.

best_available.why: Reaches the witch through a universally known story and honey through a real, if secondary, ingredient link.

pairs.pair_note: GINGERBREAD is the only workable hint; its honey side is moderate rather than immediate.

hints.reason: Bears eat honey (Pooh, 'honey bear'); bear and wolf are the classic forest predators paired in fairy tales and The Jungle Book (Baloo and the wolf pack).
Honey badger is a familiar compound; badger to wolf is only 'another wild mammal', with no shared story or phrase.

best_available.why: Strong on honey and the most natural fellow-beast to wolf.

pairs.pair_note: Both hints lean on honey compounds; BEAR has the better wolf side through shared forest/fairy-tale company.

hints.reason: Ice is frozen water; the only horse route is the water-horse Nokk in Frozen II, which is niche and needs explaining.
Icelandic horse is a real breed, but the hint contains the target ICE as a substring, a rule failure.
A one-horse open sleigh is a famous image; sleighs glide over snow and ice, a moderate ice link.

best_available.why: The only legal hint reaching both; the horse-drawn sleigh on a frozen landscape is a shared winter scene.

pairs.pair_note: ICELANDIC would have been the best clue but breaks the substring rule.

hints.reason: Horses live in stables; there is no recognisable route from stable to key (the proverb about the stable door is about the horse, not a key).
A horse bolts (verb); a key turns the bolt of a lock (deadbolt), a lock-hardware route to key.

best_available.why: Neat double meaning: the bolting horse and the bolt a key throws.

pairs.pair_note: BOLT is a genuine two-way clue; its key side goes through the lock rather than the key itself.

hints.reason: 'All the king's horses and all the king's men' in Humpty Dumpty names both words in one nursery rhyme.
'My kingdom for a horse' is a fine route, but the hint contains the target KING as a substring, a rule failure.
A knight rides a horse and serves a king; in chess the knight is the horse piece beside the king.
King Richard (Lionheart, Richard III) is a familiar royal name; the horse comes from Richard III's 'my kingdom for a horse', which many but not all players will have met.

best_available.why: One rhyme everyone knows that literally contains the king's horses.

pairs.pair_note: Rich pair; KINGDOM is lost only to the substring rule.

hints.reason: Knights joust on horseback; one scene holds both words.
Knights wear armour; warhorses in tournaments are armoured too (barding), a recognisable if secondary image.
A steed is a horse (near-synonym) and 'the knight's steed' is a stock phrase; passes but gives the horse away almost directly.
The chess knight is shaped like, and often called, the horse.

best_available.why: The most vivid single scene containing both a knight and a horse.

pairs.pair_note: Every hint passes; STEED is flagged as a near-synonym of HORSE for the owner's judgement.

hints.reason: Cavalry are horse soldiers; 'light cavalry' / the Light Brigade is a familiar military phrase.
'Dark horse' is a common compound and dark is the opposite of light.
Speed of light is a fixed phrase; horses are the archetypal fast animal (racing, galloping), a shared-property route.

best_available.why: Compound on one side, antonym on the other; both instant.

pairs.pair_note: Solid pair with three different routes.

hints.reason: Aslan the lion is Narnia's centrepiece; Narnia's talking horses (The Horse and His Boy, Bree) are a real but secondary element.
Carousel horses are iconic; lions appear on menagerie carousels but a player is unlikely to reach lion from carousel without prompting.
Both the horse and the lion are the animals famous for a mane; a textbook shared property.

best_available.why: The one physical feature these two animals uniquely share.

pairs.pair_note: MANE is excellent; CAROUSEL's lion side is real but weak.

hints.reason: Horseshoe is immediate, but the moon side exists only as a crescent-shape resemblance that no player would reach unprompted.
A mare is a female horse; the moon's dark plains are the lunar maria (Mare Tranquillitatis), a correct but specialist route.

best_available.why: The only hint with a factual route to both words, though the lunar 'mare' is niche knowledge.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. MARE is a clever clue for astronomy-literate players but too specialist to pass outright.

hints.reason: Horses are famously skittish and the mouse is the byword for timidity, but neither side is more than a mood association.
Horse stable is immediate; mice living among the hay and grain of a stable is plausible but not a scene players reach readily.
In Cinderella the fairy godmother turns the mice into horses; one story holds both.

best_available.why: The mice-into-horses transformation is one of the best-known scenes in any fairy tale.

pairs.pair_note: CINDERELLA is excellent; the other two are soft stable/mood associations.

hints.reason: The Headless Horseman rides a horse and haunts Sleepy Hollow by night.
A mare is a female horse and night+mare makes nightmare, a compound route.
Paul Revere's midnight ride was on horseback through the night; US-centric but widely taught.

best_available.why: Direct horse word that also completes NIGHTMARE.

pairs.pair_note: Strong pair; MARE is the standout.

hints.reason: Poseidon is god of the sea; he is also god of horses who created them and drives a horse-drawn chariot, a true but mythology-buff route.
Contains the target HORSE as a substring, a rule failure despite reaching both.
Ocean waves are immediate; the horse side rests on the poetic 'white horses' for breakers, which most players will not reach.
Sea is a near-synonym of ocean and sea+horse makes seahorse; a legal compound route that SEAHORSE itself breaks.

best_available.why: Does everything SEAHORSE wanted to do without containing the target.

pairs.pair_note: SEA is the legal form of the seahorse idea; POSEIDON is a good second for mythology-aware players.

hints.reason: Buccaneer is simply a pirate; nothing points to horse.
Pirates sail the sea; sea+horse makes seahorse.
A highwayman robs from horseback; he is the land-robber counterpart of the pirate, a shared outlaw category players recognise.

best_available.why: Immediate on both sides through the pirate's element and the seahorse compound.

pairs.pair_note: SEA is strong; HIGHWAYMAN is a thoughtful category route; BUCCANEER is pirate-only.

hints.reason: Royal Ascot is the horse-racing meeting the Queen famously attended each year; well known beyond Britain through the royal link.
Carriages are horse-drawn and the Queen rides in the royal carriage on state occasions.
Horse races are immediate; the Queen's love of the races is widely known, though a step removed.

best_available.why: A single image, the horse-drawn royal carriage, contains both words.

pairs.pair_note: Good pair; ASCOT and RACES share the racing route.

hints.reason: The circus ring and the circus horse act are both classic circus images.
Horse show is a familiar compound; the 'show ring' is where show horses are judged, a moderate ring link.
Horses are ridden in a riding arena; a ring (boxing, circus) is an arena, a near-synonym.

best_available.why: Ring and horse are both stock parts of the circus picture.

pairs.pair_note: All three pass; SHOW's ring side is the softest.

hints.reason: Bull reaches horse only as a fellow rodeo/ranch animal and robot only via the 'mechanical bull' ride; neither route is clear enough to count.
Westworld is a Western theme park (horses) populated by robot hosts; one title holds both for anyone who knows it.
Robots are mechanical; the coin-operated mechanical horse ride is a familiar object.

best_available.why: Horses and robots are the two defining ingredients of the franchise.

pairs.pair_note: Hard pair; WESTWORLD is pop-culture dependent and MECHANICAL's horse side is modest.

hints.reason: Rocking horse is a perfect compound, but ROCKING contains the target ROCK as a substring, a rule failure.
Crazy Horse is a famous name (Lakota leader, memorial); the rock side is only via Neil Young's band Crazy Horse being a rock act, which itself goes through 'horse'.
Horseshoe is immediate; nothing connects shoe to rock.

best_available.why: The only legal hint with any route to rock; ROCKING is the better clue but breaks the substring rule.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. The obvious clue (rocking horse) is forbidden by the substring rule; the pair needs a replacement such as a shared name or 'pet'.

hints.reason: Horses visibly sweat (lathered) and sweat is salty; a shared-property route.
A salt lick is the block horses and livestock lick; one object holds both.
Lead a horse to water; salt water is a fixed compound.

best_available.why: The salt lick is a single object that belongs to horses.

pairs.pair_note: Strong pair across three routes.

hints.reason: Horse rider is immediate; 'Shadow Riders' is an obscure novel/film and gives shadow no recognisable route.
A horse shies (verb) and horses famously shy at shadows, but shadow is reached only as the thing shied at.
A horse spooks (verb), typically at a shadow, and a spook is a ghostly shadowy figure; same scene as SHY with a slightly better shadow side.

best_available.why: Reaches horse directly and gives shadow two half-routes (the thing that spooks a horse; a spectral figure).

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. Both live hints describe the same 'horse spooked by a shadow' scene, in which shadow is only the cause.

hints.reason: Shark teeth are iconic; horse teeth are a well-known feature too (gift horse in the mouth, 'long in the tooth', horse-toothed grin).
Sharks live in the sea; sea+horse makes seahorse.

best_available.why: The seahorse compound makes the horse side as fast as the shark side.

pairs.pair_note: Both pass; TEETH is the more playful shared property.

hints.reason: Horses graze on grass; grass snake is a familiar compound (and 'snake in the grass' a stock phrase).
A horse rears up on its hind legs; a cobra rears up to strike, the same verb on both sides.

best_available.why: Instant on both sides with a compound and a phrase to help.

pairs.pair_note: Good pair; REAR is a nice shared verb.

hints.reason: Horses are kept in barns; the barn spider is a real species and Charlotte of Charlotte's Web is one, spinning her web in a barn.
Horsefly is a compound; spiders catch flies in their webs.

best_available.why: Compound on one side, the spider's prey on the other.

pairs.pair_note: Both pass; FLY is the stronger.

hints.reason: Horses jump (show jumping); to spring is to jump, a verb synonym.
The Derby is a famous horse race; its spring timing (Kentucky Derby in May) is known to racing followers but not a route most players would take.
A foal is a baby horse; foals, like lambs, are born in spring, a familiar seasonal scene.

best_available.why: Verb route that is immediate on both sides.

pairs.pair_note: JUMP is excellent; DERBY's spring side is calendar knowledge.

hints.reason: Blaze is a white facial marking and classic horse name, and stars blaze ('blazing star'); both routes are real but each is a step removed.
Trigger was Roy Rogers' horse, a dated reference, and star is reached only by calling Trigger a movie-star horse.
Pegasus is the winged horse of myth and a well-known constellation.

best_available.why: A horse that is literally among the stars.

pairs.pair_note: PEGASUS carries the pair; BLAZE is a decent horsey double meaning that needs equestrian knowledge.

hints.reason: 'You can lead a horse to water' names both words in one proverb.
'...but you can't make it drink' completes the same proverb; water is what is drunk.
A water trough is where horses drink; one object holds both.

best_available.why: The proverb everybody knows, and LEAD is the word that triggers it.

pairs.pair_note: Very strong pair.

hints.reason: Hag is a witch synonym; there is no route to horse (the worn-out horse is a 'nag', not a hag).
Witches ride brooms; a horse has no recognisable link to a broom beyond the fact that both are ridden.
You ride a horse and a witch rides her broom; a shared verb.

best_available.why: The one thing a horse and a witch's broom have in common, expressed as a verb.

pairs.pair_note: RIDE is the only two-way hint; HAG and BROOM are witch-only.

hints.reason: Wild horse is a compound (mustangs) and the wolf is the archetypal wild animal.
Wolves hunt prey; horses are classic prey animals, and wolves hunting horses is the relation between the two.
Wolf pack and packhorse are both everyday compounds.

best_available.why: Two compounds, one word.

pairs.pair_note: Strong pair; PACK is the cleanest.

hints.reason: Ice skates are immediate; iron is reached only as the metal of the blade, which few players would name.
Ice Age and Iron Age are both familiar compounds.
Ice is cold; 'cold iron' is a folklore phrase and iron feels cold to the touch, but the iron side is a soft property link.

best_available.why: Parallel compounds that land both words instantly.

pairs.pair_note: AGE is excellent; the other two are ice-first with weak iron sides.

hints.reason: Lock and key are inseparable; ice is reached only through a frozen lock in winter (de-icer) or 'ice-locked', a seasonal scene rather than a firm link.
Ice is frozen; a key is not frozen in any familiar sense (a stuck keyboard key is 'frozen' only loosely).

best_available.why: Immediate on key and gives ice the frozen-lock scene; the only hint with any two-way reach.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. The pair wants a shared compound (e.g. a word that pairs with both) which neither hint supplies.

hints.reason: Elvis is 'the King'; nothing links Elvis to ice.
The Night King of Game of Thrones is the lord of the ice-bound White Walkers; the single reference reaches king directly and ice through the character's nature, with cold nights as a fallback.
Frost is ice crystals; 'the Frost King' / Jack Frost is a familiar winter-folklore figure, a moderate king link.

best_available.why: Direct on ice with a traditional personified-king route.

pairs.pair_note: Two moderate passes, each strong on one side and fair on the other; ELVIS is king-only.

hints.reason: 'White knight' is a fixed phrase; ice and snow are the white of winter, a shared-colour route like GOLDEN for honey.
Knights wear armour; ice as armour exists only in video games and is not a recognisable route.

best_available.why: Phrase on the knight side, colour on the ice side; the only hint that reaches both.

pairs.pair_note: WHITE holds the pair on a colour route; ARMOR is knight-only.

hints.reason: Ice sparkles and sparkle is a quality of light; a shared-property verb.
Northern Lights is a fixed compound; the frozen north (Arctic ice) gives ice a recognisable geographic route.
A glacier is a river of ice; there is no route to light.

best_available.why: What ice does and what light does, in one word.

pairs.pair_note: Two good passes; GLACIER is ice-only filler.

hints.reason: Aslan is Narnia's lion; he ends the White Witch's endless winter, so the ice side comes through the frozen Narnia he thaws.
Ice Age is immediate, but the Ice Age films feature a sabre-toothed cat (Diego), not a lion, and no other route to lion exists.
Narnia is the land of eternal winter ruled over by ice until Aslan the lion returns; both words are central to the story.

best_available.why: Names the frozen world rather than just its lion, so ice and lion are equally reachable.

pairs.pair_note: Both passes come from the same story; AGE presumes a lion that is not in the film.

hints.reason: Ice is frozen; the moon is not recognisably 'frozen' to a player without the icy-moon astronomy EUROPA already carries.
Winter brings ice; 'winter moon' / the Cold Moon is a real but soft seasonal association.
Europa is Jupiter's ice-covered moon; a correct single reference reaching both for anyone with basic astronomy.

best_available.why: A real icy moon; the only hint with a firm route to both.

pairs.pair_note: EUROPA carries the pair; FROZEN and WINTER are ice-first.

hints.reason: Ice lives in the freezer; mouse has no recognisable freezer route.
Ice is frozen water; 'my mouse is frozen' is a familiar computer complaint, giving mouse a genuine everyday route.

best_available.why: The frozen computer mouse makes this the only hint that reaches both words.

pairs.pair_note: Hard pair; FROZEN's mouse side is the computer sense and should be judged on whether the owner accepts that reading.

hints.reason: Freezing makes ice; forecasts warn of an overnight freeze, so night is the time temperatures drop below freezing.
Frost is ice crystals and forms overnight ('frost tonight'); a familiar weather scene.
The Night King (Game of Thrones) is a familiar compound; Ice King (Adventure Time) and the Night King's icy nature give ice a moderate route.

best_available.why: Ice that appears in the night; immediate on both.

pairs.pair_note: All pass; FROST is the natural choice.

hints.reason: Arctic ice and the Arctic Ocean; a geographic route landing both.
An ice floe is a sheet of floating ice drifting on the ocean; the word is slightly uncommon but tied only to this scene.
Contains the target ICE as a substring, a rule failure despite the obvious ocean route.
The Titanic struck an iceberg and sank in the ocean; a universally known story holding both.

best_available.why: One story everyone knows, with ice and ocean as its two protagonists.

pairs.pair_note: Strong pair; ICEBERG fails only on the substring rule.
